output: Seven studies looked at using real-time ultrasound guidance to place catheters, which are thin tubes used to take blood samples or give medicine. In three out of seven studies, they followed good methods to make sure who got the ultrasound guidance and who got the old way. Using real-time ultrasound helped place the catheter correctly on the first try, which happened 40% less often than with the old way (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.52). It also reduced the chance of accidentally hitting an artery (RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.37) and bleeding under the skin (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.81). It also took less time to put the catheter in correctly (MD -1.40 min, 95% CI -2.17 to -0.63) and they needed fewer tries (MD -0.35, 95% CI -0.54 to -0.16) compared to the old way. Overall, using real-time ultrasound guidance seems to be better for placing catheters safely and quickly.

output: This review looked at 30 studies with 4102 patients who had kidney transplants. The study found that patients treated with tacrolimus lost fewer transplanted kidneys after six months (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.86) and this benefit lasted up to three years. However, the benefit was smaller when doctors tried to keep the medicine in the body at higher levels. Tacrolimus helped prevent acute rejection (when the body attacks the new kidney) and steroid-resistant rejection (when the body doesn't respond to medicines to stop this attack) better than cyclosporin. But it also caused more problems like needing more insulin for diabetes, having tremors, headaches, diarrhea, stomachaches, and throwing up. Cyclosporin caused more constipation and cosmetic side effects. The study didn't find any differences in infections or cancers. Overall, tacrolimus helps keep the new kidney working better and prevents some problems, but it also causes more other health issues. If 100 people got tacrolimus instead of cyclosporin, about 12 would have fewer attacks on their new kidney, 2 would lose their new kidney, but 5 to 6 would start needing extra insulin for diabetes.

output: This review looked at ten studies involving 2685 people to see if day hospital care worked as well as inpatient care for people who are sick enough to need hospitalization but not so sick that they need to stay overnight. The studies found that people in day hospitals stayed in the hospital for about the same amount of time as those in regular inpatient care. Day hospital patients also stayed a bit longer after their initial stay. Day hospital care did not seem to make people feel worse off or less happy. People also seemed to like day hospital care as much as inpatient care. While day hospitals might be just as good as regular hospitals for treating mental health problems, we still need more information to know if they are a better use of money.

output: This review looked at 46 studies with 13,451 people who had high blood pressure (BP). The studies tested different doses of a type of medicine called ARBs to see how well they lowered BP. The results show that none of the ARB medicines are clearly better or worse at lowering BP than the others. Using a dose that is 1/8 or 1/4 of the highest dose recommended by the makers of the medicine worked about 60 to 70% as well as the highest dose. Using half the highest dose worked about 80% as well. Taking even higher doses didn’t make BP go down more than the highest dose. Based on the biggest studies, the medicine lowered BP by about 8 mm Hg for systolic BP (the top number) and 5 mm Hg for diastolic BP (the bottom number) about 1 to 12 hours after taking it. The review suggests that there isn’t much difference in how well different ARB medicines work at lowering BP. The BP-lowering effect of ARBs is not very strong, and it’s about the same as another type of medicine called ACE inhibitors. Most of the BP-lowering effect happens with the lowest dose that doctors usually start with. The review couldn’t tell us much about the side effects of ARBs because the studies were short and not all reported them.

output: This review looked at 592 patients from seven studies. Larger, better-designed studies are needed to see if IS might help some patients after CABG.

output: This review looked at 34 studies of Graduated Driver Licensing (GDL) programs in different countries. These programs have rules about driving that are stricter for new drivers. output: In this review, 54 trials involving 6545 patients looked at how well interferon works to clear the virus in people with chronic hepatitis C. Patients who took interferon three times a week for 12 months had a better chance of their virus being cleared (Peto odds ratio 4.60, 95% CI 1.53 to 13.85). About 17 out of every 100 patients who took interferon had their virus completely gone after 12 months, compared to about 3 out of 100 who didn't take it. Taking more interferon or longer can help more patients get rid of the virus, but it also causes more side effects. Interferon helps improve the health of the liver in both healthy and sick livers, but it doesn't work better in people whose liver enzymes are normal. So, interferon can be helpful in clearing the virus and improving liver health, especially if taken in higher doses or for longer periods, but it's not always better for everyone.

output: This review looked at different types of hysterectomies, which are surgeries to remove the uterus. It found that subtotal hysterectomy (TH) and total hysterectomy (STH) did not make much difference in how well women could urinate, have bowel movements, or have sex after the surgery. The operations took about 11 minutes shorter and caused less bleeding with TH. Women who had TH were less likely to get a fever or have trouble peeing right after the surgery. However, they were more likely to have bleeding that comes and goes (cyclical bleeding) for up to a year after the surgery. There was no clear difference in other problems like needing stitches or having to go back to the hospital. Overall, the review suggests that TH does not offer better results for urinary, bowel, or sexual function compared to STH. Women might be more likely to have ongoing bleeding after TH.

output: This review looked at 22 studies involving 6872 women and their babies. Antibiotics given after a woman has premature labour (PROM) seem to help reduce a condition called chorioamnionitis, which can make the baby sick. Babies born within 48 hours and up to 7 days after the study started also tend to be healthier. Antibiotics also seem to lower the chance of babies needing extra medicine to breathe, extra oxygen, or having problems with their brains. However, one type of antibiotic called co-amoxiclav might cause a serious problem in the baby's tummy. When it comes to the long-term health of the children, there isn't enough information to know if antibiotics help. But since antibiotics can help babies feel better in the short term, doctors usually prescribe them. It's important to note that co-amoxiclav should not be used because it might cause a problem in the baby's tummy.

output: This review looked at 33 studies with 2973 children who had diarrhea. Most studies were done in richer countries. Some studies looked at babies under 12 months old, and others didn't include breastfed babies. The studies found that switching to lactose-free milk or milk products might help diarrhea go away faster by about 18 hours. It also seems to help stop the diarrhea less often. But, changing to diluted milk didn't seem to help diarrhea go away faster. It might help stop diarrhea less often though. For young children who aren't mostly breastfed, changing to a lactose-free diet might make diarrhea go away sooner and help it stop less often. However, more studies are needed to be sure about this. There are no studies from poorer countries where diarrhea can be more dangerous and where kids might be more likely to be malnourished.

output: This review looked at 68 studies where people took aspirin doses ranging from 300 mg to 1200 mg. Most people took 600/650 mg or 990/1000 mg. The studies were generally well done. For people with moderate to severe pain, taking aspirin helped reduce their pain faster than taking a sugar pill. The type of pain didn't affect how well aspirin worked. Lower doses didn't help much. Taking higher doses of aspirin was more effective but also caused more side effects like feeling dizzy, sleepy, or having stomach problems. Paracetamol works similarly to aspirin for pain relief. Overall, aspirin is a good medicine to use for pain, especially if you take it at higher doses, but you need to be careful about the side effects. The benefits and risks haven't changed since the last review.

output: This review looked at 23 studies involving 188,934 young people in the USA, Canada, and Australia from 1991 to 2012. Most of the studies were done well, but some had problems. The studies tried to see if media campaigns could help reduce drug use among young people. Five studies that randomly picked who got the campaign and who didn't found no difference in drug use. Four studies that watched changes over time also saw no clear effect. But one study found that a campaign might have reduced methamphetamine use among 12 to 17-year-olds. Other studies had mixed results. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say if media campaigns work to reduce drug use in young people. More studies are needed to find out.

output: This review looked at seven studies involving 1919 people who play sports regularly. Many of these studies had problems like not being blinded or missing some information. Four studies tried special exercises to prevent hamstring injuries, but the results were mixed. Two studies found that doing extra hamstring exercises didn't help prevent injuries, while one small study suggested it might, but the control group had mostly minor injuries. Another study using manual therapy (like gentle hands-on treatment) seemed to help prevent lower limb muscle strains, but not hamstring injuries. Three other studies tested different ways to prevent lower leg injuries, but none found a clear way to prevent hamstring injuries. Overall, there isn't enough good evidence to know if any specific methods work best to prevent hamstring injuries in sports. The findings about manual therapy need more research to confirm.

output: In this review, 79 studies involving 24,308 participants looked at how well the collaborative care model worked for adults with depression and anxiety. However, it didn't seem to help people's physical health as much. Overall, the collaborative care model seems to be a helpful extra part of treatment for adults who have depression and anxiety.

output: This review looked at six studies with about 450 patients. Most studies were well done, but none were completely blinded because the treatment involved inserting something into the body. After one year, more patients kept their limbs when they got special electrical devices (SCS) compared to those who just used regular treatments. Patients in the SCS group also felt less pain and got better faster. More patients in the SCS group reached a stage where they could walk around more easily. While the SCS didn't help wounds heal faster, it caused fewer problems like the device getting stuck or needing to be fixed again. About 17 out of every 100 patients had minor problems with the SCS, which means it might be worth it. The SCS cost more money over two years, about €36,500 compared to €28,600 for regular treatments. So, while the SCS helped keep limbs and reduced pain, it might not be the best choice for everyone because of the small chance of problems and higher cost.

output: This review looked at two studies that compared two ways of starting medicine called cART in children with HIV. Both studies were done in countries like Thailand and Cambodia. The first study started cART right away for children who were sick, while the second study waited until their CD4 count (a measure of how well the immune system is working) dropped below 15%. In the first study, there was one death in the group that started cART right away, but no deaths in the group that waited. When looking at children who were about 2 to 5 years old, there were no more deaths in either group. The second study found that waiting to start cART didn't affect the number of serious health problems. Another study from South Africa looked at children starting medicine for another illness called TB and found that waiting more than 60 days to start cART might make it harder for children to stay healthy. Overall, the studies don't clearly show whether it's better to start cART right away or wait based on CD4 counts. More research is needed to decide the best way to start this important medicine for children with HIV.

output: This review looked at four studies involving 571 women who had surgery for gynecological cancers. The studies found that putting a tube drain in the area where the lymph nodes were removed did not help prevent fluid-filled cysts (lymphocysts) right after surgery. The studies had some limitations, so we're not completely sure about the results, especially for the cysts that cause symptoms. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: Six studies looked at how people feel after donating stem cells for someone else. Most people who donated either bone marrow or peripheral blood felt some pain. Bone marrow donors often had more pain at the donation site and more health problems overall. They also had to stay home from work more days than those who donated peripheral blood stem cells. Peripheral blood donors sometimes had more pain before donating, which might be because they got a medicine called G-CSF beforehand. The studies weren't perfect and didn't always tell us why some donors weren't included. Bone marrow donors generally had more pain and less time at work after donating compared to peripheral blood donors. But because the studies weren't very good, we can't be sure if these differences mean anything important. More research is needed to understand the long-term effects and how to make donating easier for everyone.

output: Seven trials with 380 children who had a very bad asthma attack and had to go to the hospital showed that adding a medicine called aminophylline to other medicines like steroids and bronchodilators (which help open airways) helped their breathing better. The medicine worked quickly, improving how well their lungs were working after 6 to 8 hours. It also helped their quick flow rate of air (PEF) improve more than the other medicine. However, it didn't make the children feel better faster, have fewer nebulizer treatments, or stay in the hospital less. There wasn't enough information to know if it helped with oxygen levels or how long they needed extra oxygen. Using aminophylline also made children more likely to vomit. While it helped breathing, it didn't seem to reduce other asthma symptoms or the need for hospital stays. More research is needed to see if it affects things like needing to stay in the ICU or use a ventilator.

output: This review looked at different ways to remove cataracts, which are cloudy spots in the eye that can make it hard to see clearly. The study found that a method called phacoemulsification works better than another method called extracapsular surgery (ECCE) for improving vision. Another method, called manual small incision surgery, also helps people see better than ECCE but not as well as phacoemulsification. The study suggests that phacoemulsification might be the best choice for seeing clearly, but it's more expensive. ECCE with a lens inside the eye is a good option too and is easier to use in clinics. More research is needed to compare the long-term effects of these methods, especially in places where they might be cheaper.

More research is needed to understand these issues better.

output: This review looked at 62 studies with 1982 participants who had mirror therapy compared to other treatments after having a stroke. Most studies lasted about 4 weeks and happened 3 to 7 times a week for 30 minutes each. Mirror therapy helped people move better and less disabled, especially if their usual treatment wasn't as good. There were some problems with the studies, like not always following the same rules, so we're not completely sure how well mirror therapy works. Overall, mirror therapy seems to be helpful for improving movement, disability, and pain, but more research is needed to be really confident.

output: Two studies looked at a technique called in vitro maturation (IVM) for treating infertility in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome. Both studies were done in ways that made it hard to know if they were fair and unbiased. They didn't show clear results about whether IVM helps more than another method called in vitro fertilization (IVF). The studies did find that more women who had IVM became pregnant than those who had IVF. Neither study found any cases of a serious side effect called ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. While the results are promising, the studies weren't perfect and the evidence isn't strong enough to make any new rules about using IVM. We're waiting for results from six more studies that are still going on. When those results come out, we'll have better information to help decide if IVM might be helpful for some women with this condition.

output: A study found that using a special device called a cervical pessary during pregnancy helped prevent premature births. This study involved 385 pregnant women whose cervixes were shorter than normal. The women who used the pessary had a much lower chance of having a baby born too early (less than 37 weeks) compared to those who waited to see if the baby would come naturally. Specifically, 22% of women using the pessary had a premature birth, compared to 59% of those waiting. The babies born to women using the pessary were also born later, on average, at 37.7 weeks compared to 34.9 weeks for those waiting. Using the pessary also meant fewer medicines to help the baby stay in the womb and fewer steroid shots to help the baby's lungs grow faster. However, more women using the pessary had a type of vaginal discharge. About 27 women needed their pessary to be moved, and one woman needed it removed. Most women who used the pessary said they would recommend it to others. Babies born to women using the pessary were less likely to need special care after birth. While this study suggests the pessary might be helpful, more research is needed in different places and with different types of pregnancies to be sure.

Overall, the evidence suggests that starting statins soon after having ACS doesn't help prevent major heart problems like death, heart attack, or stroke, but it might help prevent unstable chest pain. This review looked at six studies that tested whether giving lactoferrin to babies through their food helps prevent a serious infection called sepsis and another condition called necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). The studies found that giving lactoferrin might help reduce sepsis and NEC. Specifically:

- It reduced sepsis by about half (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.87) and NEC by about a quarter (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.86).
- It didn't seem to affect death (all-cause mortality) or how long babies stayed in the hospital.
- When lactoferrin was given along with probiotics (another type of good bacteria), it helped even more with sepsis and NEC.
- Giving lactoferrin with probiotics also seemed to reduce certain types of infections like bacterial and fungal sepsis.
- There were no serious side effects reported.
- The studies had some limitations, so the evidence is considered of low quality.
- More studies are needed to confirm these findings and to learn more about the best way to use lactoferrin.
- Longer-term studies are also needed to see if giving lactoferrin affects how well babies do later in life.

So, combining insulin with oral medicine at night seems to work well for controlling blood sugar and helps with weight.

output: We looked for studies comparing different treatments for a type of cancer called GTN, but we couldn't find any. This is because GTN is rare and often responds well to chemotherapy. For people whose cancer doesn't respond to the first treatment, doctors usually give a combination of drugs like methotrexate, dactinomycin, and other medicines. However, giving dactinomycin for five days at a time can cause more side effects than giving it in shorter bursts. So, we think it would be helpful to do a study comparing these two ways of giving dactinomycin. For more advanced cases, a common treatment is a combination of methotrexate, dactinomycin, and other drugs. But we're not sure if another combination of drugs might work just as well with fewer side effects. We need more research to figure out the best treatment for people whose cancer keeps coming back. It would be hard to do this kind of study in one country, so working together with other countries might help us get the information we need. Future research should also look at how much these treatments cost and check for any new cancers that might develop later.

output: This review looked at 22 studies comparing different breathing methods for babies born prematurely. The studies found that using HFPPV (a type of breathing method) or triggered ventilation (where the machine helps breathe at certain times) might help reduce air leaks and shorten how long babies need to be on a breathing machine. However, these methods didn't seem to make babies healthier overall. Babies who got HFPPV had a slightly lower chance of getting a lung problem called BPD, but triggered ventilation seemed to make BPD more likely. Babies on triggered ventilation also stayed on the breathing machine for longer. While these methods might help, more research is needed to confirm their benefits and to make sure they don't cause other problems. It's important to test these methods carefully in larger studies before using them widely.

Since the last time this review was done, no new studies were found. While HDR ICBT has some potential advantages like better accuracy and patient convenience, it didn't show a clear benefit over LDR ICBT in terms of survival or other important outcomes. Because the studies had some flaws, we can't be very sure about the results. We still recommend using HDR ICBT for treating all stages of cervical cancer because of its benefits. More well-designed studies are needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at 63 trials with 9168 participants to see if antidepressants called SSRIs help people recover from a stroke. Right now, there's not enough good evidence to say that SSRIs should be used to help people recover from a stroke. More research is needed to see if SSRIs might help some people.

Some newborns might get sick from DPNB, like having trouble swallowing or getting a small bruise, but these are rare. EMLA can cause a few minor problems like feeling sick or having a red face, but it's usually safe. Neither DPNB nor EMLA fully stops the pain, but they do help a lot. DPNB seems to work best overall.

The amount of eplerenone taken each day varied from 25 mg to 400 mg. When we added up the results from all the studies, we found that eplerenone helped lower blood pressure. It reduced systolic blood pressure (the top number) by about 9.21 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure (the bottom number) by about 4.18 mmHg. This happened whether people took 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg, or 400 mg of eplerenone each day. Eplerenone helps lower blood pressure, but we don't know if it affects things like death or illness. We also don't have enough information to know if eplerenone causes problems for people's health. More studies are needed to learn more.

output: This review looked at eight studies that compared different treatments for a type of blood cancer called follicular lymphoma (FL). The studies involved 2636 patients who had never received treatment for their cancer. Most studies lasted between three and five years. The studies found that adding a medicine called anti-CD20 (ACR) to chemotherapy did not improve overall survival, but it might help keep the cancer under control longer. Adding anthracyclines, another type of chemotherapy, did not seem to help overall survival, but it might help keep the cancer under control better. The studies also found that anthracyclines were linked to some heart problems, though these were rare. The evidence is not very strong because the studies weren't always done the same way or were a bit old. More research is needed to see if adding ACR to chemotherapy helps people with FL live longer or feel better.

output: This review looked at 25 studies that were done well. Some studies used a medicine called sitagliptin, and others used another called vildagliptin. About 6743 people took sitagliptin and 6121 took vildagliptin. Both medicines helped lower blood sugar levels, about 0.7% and 0.6% respectively, compared to a sugar pill. When compared to other medicines that lower blood sugar, sitagliptin and vildagliptin didn't seem to work better. These medicines didn't cause people to gain weight, but they sometimes caused people to lose weight. They didn't cause more problems with the pancreas, which makes insulin. Both medicines were safe to take, but people taking them had more infections. It's not clear if these medicines help prevent heart problems or death. More studies are needed to know if these medicines are safe and effective in the long run. We also need more information about how these medicines affect things like quality of life and the risk of getting diabetes-related problems.

output: This review looked at 44 studies comparing dietary advice to no advice for people with heart problems. About 52,000 people took part in these studies. The studies showed that people who got dietary advice had lower levels of bad cholesterol (LDL) and total cholesterol compared to those who didn't get advice. Their blood pressure also went down a little bit. People who got advice ate more fruits and vegetables and less fat and saturated fat. Some studies found that people who got advice ate more fiber and less salt. However, the studies had some problems because people might not have told the truth about what they ate. Also, the studies lasted different lengths of time, which made it hard to know if the benefits would last. Overall, dietary advice seems to help improve diet and some heart health markers, but we don't know if it will help prevent heart problems in the long run. More research is needed to find out.

output: This review looked at 24 studies with 3377 people to see if pentoxifylline helps with a condition called intermittent claudication, which makes walking painful. Most of the studies weren't very good at making sure everyone got fair chances to get better. The studies also didn't always tell us if they followed the right rules to make sure the results were fair. The studies varied a lot, so it's hard to combine their results. More high-quality studies are needed to find out if pentoxifylline is helpful for people with this condition.

output: Two small studies looked at using a medicine called lorazepam to help reduce confusion (delirium) in patients with serious illnesses. In one study, patients with advanced cancer who were in a special care unit were given lorazepam along with another medicine called haloperidol. The study found that lorazepam didn't seem to make much difference in how severe the confusion was, how long the patients stayed in the hospital, or how many patients died. The study also didn't tell us how long the confusion lasted. In another study, patients with AIDS who were in regular hospital rooms were given lorazepam, another medicine called chlorpromazine, or still another medicine called haloperidol. Again, the study found that lorazepam didn't seem to make much difference in how severe the confusion was, how long the patients stayed in the hospital, or how many patients died. The study also didn't tell us how long the confusion lasted. Based on these studies, we don't have enough information to say if lorazepam is helpful or harmful when used to treat confusion in patients who aren't in the ICU. More research is needed to find out if lorazepam might be useful for treating confusion in patients like these.

output: This review looked at eight studies with 948 participants to see if giving corticosteroids (a type of steroid medicine) helps treat dengue, a disease spread by mosquitoes. The studies looked at children and adults with dengue who had different stages of the illness. For those with dengue-related shock, the studies didn't find that corticosteroids helped reduce deaths, blood transfusions, lung bleeding, seizures, or how long they stayed in the hospital. For those with early-stage dengue, the studies didn't show that corticosteroids helped prevent death, severe dengue, bleeding, low platelets, fluid buildup, or needing ICU care. The studies are quite old and had some problems, so we can't be sure if corticosteroids help or not. There isn't enough good-quality evidence to know if corticosteroids work for early-stage dengue or dengue-related shock. More studies are needed to find out.

output: This review looked at nine studies with 825 people who took part in the studies. output: Three small studies with a total of 50 participants looked at whether taking resveratrol, a substance found in grapes and red wine, helps people with type 2 diabetes. The studies lasted about four to five weeks and gave different amounts of resveratrol—10 mg, 150 mg, or 1000 mg each day. None of the studies had problems being fair in their comparisons (low risk of bias). The studies didn’t look at long-term effects like death or serious health problems. They also didn’t report on things like how well people felt or if they had side effects. The studies found that resveratrol didn’t seem to help lower blood sugar levels (glycosylated haemoglobin A1c) or blood sugar after eating (fasting blood glucose) better than a sugar pill. The studies were too short to know if resveratrol might help. Some studies found that resveratrol might make insulin resistance (a condition where the body doesn’t use insulin properly) a tiny bit worse, but it’s hard to tell because the studies were small. Right now, there isn’t enough good research to say if resveratrol helps or hurts people with type 2 diabetes. More studies are needed to find out if resveratrol works and if it’s safe for people with type 2 diabetes. These studies would need to last longer and look at important health outcomes.

output: This review looked at 22 studies that tested different supplements and medicines for people with schizophrenia. Most studies lasted about 8 weeks. The evidence isn't strong enough to tell if these supplements work or not. More studies with longer follow-up times are needed to get clearer answers.

output: This review looked at eight studies involving 1470 adults and 470 children. The studies had mixed quality and varied in how severe the asthma flare-ups were. For oral treatments, there wasn't much difference between LTRAs (a type of medicine) and regular care in terms of needing extra help or hospital visits. However, LTRAs seemed to improve breathing tests (measuring lung function) in some studies. Headaches were the most common side effect, but they weren't different between the groups. When looking at IV treatments (given through a vein), there was a slight chance that LTRAs might lower the risk of needing hospital care. But the difference in breathing tests wasn't clear. Overall, the current evidence doesn't strongly support using LTRA medicines regularly for acute asthma. More studies are needed to see if IV treatments can prevent hospital stays and to find the best way to use these medicines safely and effectively.

This review looked at 34 studies with 8635 participants to see how well Portable Opsonin Collection System (POCS) works in detecting injuries in the chest and abdomen. Overall, POCS was about 74% sensitive (meaning it correctly identified 74% of the actual injuries) and 96% specific (meaning it correctly identified 96% of the people who didn't have injuries). But the results varied depending on who the study was done in—adults, children, or mixed populations. 

For adults or mixed populations, POCS was better at finding injuries in the chest (96% accurate) and abdomen (97% accurate). But for children, it was less accurate, finding injuries 63% of the time and missing 118 children with injuries. 

If POCS says someone has an injury, it's usually right, but if it says someone doesn't have an injury, it might be wrong sometimes. So, for chest injuries, POCS helps doctors decide if treatment is needed. But for abdominal injuries, POCS alone isn't enough; doctors need to use other tests like CT scans to make sure there aren't any hidden injuries. 

For children, POCS isn't very good at finding injuries in the abdomen. More studies are needed to confirm if POCS is better at finding chest injuries.

output: This review looked at 85 studies involving 10,350 patients who had elective surgery. Most studies were done in different parts of the world, including high-, middle-, and low-income countries. About 82 studies had enough information to be combined in a big picture look at the results. Five studies had some issues that might have affected their results. Lidocaine, a medicine that numbs skin, was added to propofol, another medicine used during surgery, to see if it helped reduce pain. Adding lidocaine to propofol reduced pain after the injection by about half compared to using just propofol. Pretreating patients with lidocaine also helped reduce pain. Both adding lidocaine to propofol and giving it to patients before the injection worked well. The side effects of lidocaine were rare. The quality of the evidence from these studies is very good. Based on these studies, we know that both ways of using lidocaine work well to reduce pain during surgery, and there's no clear difference between the two methods.

This review looked at five studies, but three of them didn't have enough useful information. So, we only had data from two studies with 105 people to look at. We couldn't compare everything like death rates or costs, but we did find some helpful information:

- Both studies also showed that people's heart problems got better. For example, people who got special pacing had their heart problems rated lower (from 2.5 to 2.2) compared to those who got a placebo (from 2.6 to 1.7).

They mostly focused on how well the heart worked, but didn't look at important things like whether people lived longer or if the treatments were worth the cost. output: This review looked at seven studies about exercising to help people with HIV/AIDS. The studies were different in how they were done, so it's hard to combine their results. Most studies showed that doing exercises like lifting weights or walking regularly for at least four weeks might help people with HIV/AIDS gain a little bit of weight and muscle. Some studies also found that these exercises can make it easier for people to breathe and move around. The studies suggested that these exercises can help people with HIV/AIDS feel stronger and less stressed. None of the studies showed that these exercises caused any serious problems. However, the results are based on just a few studies, and the studies had different ways of measuring things. So, while these exercises seem safe and might help, we need more research with more people to be sure. Future studies should include more women, older people, and people at different stages of HIV to get a better idea of how well these exercises work. Also, studies should follow people longer and include everyone who started the exercise program, even if they stop later, to get a clearer picture of how well these exercises work.

output: This review looked at studies comparing two ways to keep kidneys healthy after a transplant. Most studies compared a method called HMP (High Machine Perfusion) with another called SCS (Standard Care). The main finding is that HMP seems to reduce a condition called Delayed Graft Function (DGF), which happens when the new kidney doesn't work right right after the transplant. HMP helps prevent DGF better than SCS, especially in kidneys from people who died recently. It's been shown to work well in recent studies using a special machine. HMP might also save money and help the new kidney last longer. However, we don't know if it makes a big difference in other things like how quickly the new kidney starts working or how long it lasts. More studies are needed to look specifically at how HMP affects DGF and to see if it works as well in the long run. We also need more research to confirm if HMP is better than SCS for preventing DGF and to understand its effects on other important outcomes.

output: This review looked at studies about surgery for advanced-stage ovarian cancer. It found that removing as much of the cancer as possible (complete cytoreduction) helps women live longer. When doctors can't remove all the cancer, getting rid of as little as possible (optimal cytoreduction) is still better than leaving more behind. But the studies weren't perfect because they didn't follow all the rules to make sure they were fair. The review suggests that during surgery for advanced ovarian cancer, doctors should try to remove all the cancer they can. If they can't, they should aim to remove as little as possible. More studies are needed to figure out if it's the surgery itself or other things like how sick the person is that makes a big difference in how long they live. The review also recommends calling the amount of cancer left after surgery "near optimal" instead of "optimal" to avoid confusion.

output: This review looked at 56 studies involving 204,759 pregnancies, including 2113 with Down's syndrome. Most studies were done well, but some only tested high-risk pregnancies. Researchers looked at 78 different test combinations using various markers like PAPP-A, free βhCG, and AFP. They found that a test strategy combining maternal age and a double marker combination of PAPP-A and free βhCG worked best. This strategy helps find about 7 out of every 10 pregnancies with Down's syndrome without too many false alarms. Adding more markers didn't seem to improve the test. Parents need to think about this when deciding if they want these tests.

The review found that giving people 14 days of primaquine each day worked well to stop malaria from coming back. Smaller doses of primaquine for shorter periods didn't work as well. More studies are needed to see if shorter, less frequent doses of primaquine are as good as the standard 14-day dose.

This review looked at eight studies that tested whether taking folic acid and/or vitamin B12 helps improve thinking skills and mood in older people. The studies were different in how they were done, so it wasn't possible to combine their results. 

For healthy older people without memory problems, there isn't enough good evidence to say that taking folic acid helps their thinking skills or mood. But in one study of older people with higher-than-normal levels of a substance called homocysteine, taking 800 mcg of folic acid each day for three years seemed to help with overall functioning, memory, and how fast they process information.

For people with memory problems like Alzheimer's, taking 1 mg of folic acid each day seemed to make the medicine they take to help their memory work better. It also seemed to help with their ability to do daily tasks and their behavior.

However, for people with memory problems who don't have high homocysteine levels, taking folic acid didn't seem to help their thinking skills. And for both healthy older people and those with memory problems, taking folic acid alone didn't seem to help much.

Taking folic acid and vitamin B12 together did help lower a substance called homocysteine in the blood, which is good for the heart. Taking folic acid was generally safe, with few side effects.

Overall, the studies don't give us clear answers about whether folic acid helps older people's thinking skills. More research is needed to find out if folic acid can help people with memory problems.

output: This review looked at 16 studies with 26,795 older adults (average age 73 years) who had high blood pressure. Most of these adults were taking a common medicine called a thiazide diuretic. The review found that taking this medicine reduced their chances of dying from any cause by about 11%, compared to those not taking it. It also reduced their chances of having heart problems like heart attacks and strokes by about 38%. However, more people stopped taking the medicine because of side effects. The benefits were seen mainly in adults aged 60 to 79 years. The review suggests that treating older adults with high blood pressure can help prevent heart problems and death, especially in the younger part of this age group. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

This study looked at a test called SPECT scanning using a special tracer called 123I-FP-CIT to see if it can help diagnose a condition called DLB, which is a type of Alzheimer's disease. The study involved 22 people who might have DLB or Alzheimer's disease. The test was done twice: once to see how well it works and again to see how often it correctly identifies DLB. 

For the first time, the test showed that it can correctly identify DLB about 100% of the time (very good) when looking at the whole picture. When just looking at the pictures, it still identified DLB correctly about 86% of the time. This suggests the test is very good at finding DLB.

The study found that the test is better at diagnosing DLB than doctors' guesses alone. But, because the study was small, the results aren't very precise. Overall, the test seems to be very helpful in diagnosing DLB, especially when people are strongly suspected of having it. However, more research is needed to confirm these findings and to see how well the test works in people with milder forms of dementia.

Overall, the Epley manoeuvre seems to be a good, safe way to treat BPPV. It works better than other similar movements, but it doesn't always fix the problem completely. About 36% of people still get BPPV again after treatment.

This review looked at ten studies involving 813 participants to see if propofol, a medicine used to help people sleep during certain medical procedures, caused more side effects or made people less satisfied compared to other medicines. Some studies only included children, others only adults, and one included both. Most of the studies had some problems that might have affected their results. 

One study found that people who got propofol with another medicine called midazolam had more nightmares and changes in behavior after the procedure compared to those who got another combination of medicines. But seven other studies didn't find any difference in side effects between propofol and other medicines. 

For pain at the injection site, four studies didn't find any difference. And for how satisfied people were with the procedure, four studies didn't find any difference either. 

All the studies used propofol without adding extra pain relief, and most had fewer than 100 people in them. Because the studies were different and had small numbers, it's hard to know if propofol causes more side effects or makes people less satisfied. The evidence isn't strong enough to draw clear conclusions about using propofol with or without extra pain relief for people getting a procedure in the emergency room. More studies with larger groups of people would be helpful.

output: In this review, 50 studies looked at different ways to help people stop smoking after they leave the hospital. Intensive counselling that starts during hospital stays and continues for at least a month after discharge helped people quit smoking more often than usual care. This was true even if everyone got the same amount of counselling in the hospital. Adding nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) to intensive counselling worked better than just intensive counselling alone. But adding varenicline or bupropion to intensive counselling didn't seem to help more people quit. Intensive counselling that includes counselling and sometimes medicine worked best for people who were admitted to the hospital because of heart problems. It helped more people stop smoking and also reduced their chances of getting sick or needing to go back to the hospital. This type of intensive counselling worked in both regular hospitals and special rehabilitation centers. Adding NRT to intensive counselling seemed to help more people stop smoking. But there wasn't enough information to know if adding varenicline or bupropion to intensive counselling would help more people quit smoking.

output: This review looked at eight studies involving 6615 people to see if sending text messages helped them keep their doctor’s appointments. Four new studies were found. The studies showed that getting text message reminders made people show up to their doctor’s appointments more often than not getting any reminders. This happened whether the reminders came via text or phone calls. Combining text messages with regular mail reminders worked even better. People who got text messages showed up to appointments 80.3% of the time, compared to 78.6% for those who got just text messages and 67.8% for those who got no reminders. None of the studies found any bad side effects from the reminders. Some studies said it cost less to send text messages than make phone calls. But the studies didn’t look at how well the reminders actually helped people feel better or if the reminders caused any problems. The evidence is not strong enough to know if text message reminders really help people keep their appointments or if they’re worth using. More studies are needed to find out. These studies should look at things like how well the reminders work, how much they cost, and if they cause any problems. They should also tell us what the reminders say and when they’re sent.

Overall, the evidence suggests that acupuncture might help with some symptoms of schizophrenia, but it's not clear if it works better than other treatments. More studies are needed to know for sure.

Most of the studies had some problems keeping everything fair, like not making sure doctors didn't know who got which treatment.

Total thyroidectomy was better at preventing a condition called recurrent hyperthyroidism, where the thyroid gland starts working too much again after it was removed. It was also better at preventing this in people who had the Dunhill procedure. However, total thyroidectomy was linked to a higher chance of a condition called permanent hypocalcaemia/hypoparathyroidism, where the body doesn't make enough calcium. This wasn't seen when people had bilateral subtotal thyroidectomy.

The studies didn't look at how well people felt or if the surgeries affected their eyes or voice. One person died in a study, but the researchers didn't have more information about why. The review suggests that total thyroidectomy might be better at preventing hyperthyroidism, but it's not clear if it affects other things like quality of life. More studies are needed to find out.

This review looked at four studies with 253 people who had a condition called pilonidal sinus disease. The studies compared different ways to treat it, using things like a special glue called fibrin glue. Here’s what they found:

- Using fibrin glue instead of another treatment called Bascom's procedure might help reduce pain right after the procedure (a bit), but the evidence isn't very strong.
- Fibrin glue might help people get back to normal activities faster than Bascom's procedure (about 3 weeks faster).
- When used with a type of surgery called the Limberg flap, fibrin glue might make the wound heal faster (by about 14 days).
- It's not clear if fibrin glue helps prevent a common problem called postoperative seroma, which is when fluid builds up in the wound.
- Fibrin glue might also help with pain and getting back to normal activities faster when used with the Limberg flap.
- Adding fibrin glue to the Limberg flap might help people leave the hospital sooner.
- There wasn’t enough information to know if fibrin glue works better than other treatments for preventing a complication called seroma or for reducing the length of time someone stays in the hospital.
- The studies were small and had some problems, so the results aren’t very strong. More and better studies are needed to understand if fibrin glue really helps with these conditions.

This study looked at three trials that tested different antibiotic treatments for women having normal births. The trials happened in different places and times, mostly in the 1960s and 1990s. The main finding was that women who got antibiotics had a lower chance of getting a type of infection called endometritis, which is an infection of the lining of the uterus. This was true in two out of the three trials, but the evidence isn't very strong because there weren't many women in the study and the results were a bit uncertain. 

There wasn't much difference between the groups for other types of infections like urinary tract infections or wound infections. The women who got antibiotics stayed in the hospital for about the same amount of time. Antibiotics cost more money, about twice as much.

The trials didn't look at whether antibiotics caused side effects or if they helped women feel better. They also didn't check if using antibiotics made it harder for germs to become resistant to medicines. 

While antibiotics might help prevent one type of infection, they don't seem to help with other types of infections or make women stay in the hospital longer. It's important to use antibiotics carefully because overusing them can lead to germs becoming resistant to medicine. More studies are needed to see if giving antibiotics to all women after normal births is helpful.

output: This review looked at 177 studies with 34,808 participants to see if certain treatments helped with psoriasis. For most vitamin D medicines applied to the body, they worked better than a sugar pill. This means people felt better, with scores improving by about 0.8 to 1.9 points on a scale. Potent and very potent corticosteroids also worked well, helping people feel better by about 1.0 to 1.8 points. Other treatments like dithranol, combined vitamin D and corticosteroid, and tazarotene were also better than a sugar pill. When comparing vitamin D to strong corticosteroids, the results were mixed. But when using both vitamin D and corticosteroid together, it worked better than just vitamin D or just corticosteroid. Vitamin D was less effective for scalp psoriasis compared to strong corticosteroids. Strong corticosteroids caused fewer skin problems like burning or irritation. They were also easier to use than vitamin D alone. However, there's not enough information to know if using strong corticosteroids long-term might cause changes to the skin. More research is needed to understand this better and to find safe ways to treat psoriasis over time.

output: This review looked at 100 studies involving more than 83,000 mother-infant pairs. Most of the studies had some issues in how they were done, but the overall picture is clear: extra support for mothers helps keep them breastfeeding longer and more exclusively. This support can come from doctors, nurses, or other helpers. Studies show that extra support reduces the chances of moms stopping breastfeeding altogether, and also keeps moms from stopping exclusive breastfeeding (when only breast milk is given). The benefits are seen whether the support comes from professionals or non-professionals, or both. To work best, the support should be offered regularly, like once every few weeks, and tailored to the mom's needs and the place where she lives. It's also helpful if the support is given by someone who has talked to the mom before, like her doctor or nurse. Overall, extra support seems to help moms keep breastfeeding longer and more exclusively.

While ultrasound didn't seem to affect the overall success rate or the number of complications, it did help in some specific areas like reducing the risk of bleeding and making the first attempt more successful. However, the evidence wasn't strong enough to compare how well ultrasound works for experienced or inexperienced doctors or for people who might have a higher risk of complications. More research is needed to fully understand the benefits of using ultrasound in these situations.

output: This review looked at three trials involving 20,412 women who had heavy bleeding after childbirth (postpartum haemorrhage or PPH). Two of the trials compared a medicine called tranexamic acid (TXA) given through a vein (intravenous) with a placebo or usual care. Overall, the evidence suggests that omega-3 fatty acids might help prevent the transition to psychosis, but more research is needed to confirm this. Other treatments didn't show a clear benefit in preventing this transition.

This review looked at different ways to help prevent altitude sickness (AMS) before going to high altitudes. It included 20 studies with 1406 participants. Some methods like using a special machine to simulate altitude or a technique called remote ischaemic preconditioning didn't seem to help prevent AMS. For supplements and vitamins, taking certain things like antioxidants, medroxyprogesterone, iron, or Rhodiola crenulata didn't seem to help prevent AMS. However, taking erythropoietin might help, but the evidence isn't strong because the study had some problems. When ginkgo biloba was taken with another medicine called acetazolamide, it seemed to help prevent AMS, but again, the evidence is not very strong. Taking medroxyprogesterone with acetazolamide didn't seem to help prevent AMS.

Overall, the evidence is mixed and not very strong. More studies are needed to better understand if these methods work and if they're safe. Clinicians should use caution and consider the quality of the evidence when recommending these methods.

This review looked at 28 studies comparing different ways to keep patients asleep during surgery. Most of the studies used propofol and others used gases like sevoflurane, isoflurane, and desflurane. Many studies didn't clearly describe how they picked who got which treatment, which made it hard to know if the results are reliable. About half of the studies couldn't tell if the people giving out medicine knew who was getting which treatment, which might have affected the results. 

The studies mostly found that using propofol to keep patients asleep didn't make it more likely that they would have problems like confusion after surgery (postoperative delirium). But the evidence for this isn't very strong because the studies weren't very big or clear. There wasn't enough evidence to say if propofol kept people from having more problems after surgery (POCD) or if it changed how long they stayed in the hospital.

Some studies suggested that propofol might help with POCD, but the evidence wasn't very strong. There wasn't enough evidence to say if propofol or other medicines used to keep patients asleep changed how long it took for patients to wake up after surgery (length of stay in the PACU) or if it changed how long they stayed in the hospital.

Overall, the evidence isn't very strong about whether propofol or other medicines used to keep patients asleep affect these things. More studies are needed to get a clearer picture.

This review looked at 60 trials involving 3620 people with chronic rotator cuff problems. Most of the trials had low risk of bias, but some had unclear or high risk. Only one trial compared manual therapy and exercise to a placebo, and it showed that these treatments helped reduce pain and improve function more than the placebo. About 7 out of 10 people who got manual therapy and exercise said their condition improved, compared to about 4 out of 10 who got the placebo. The treatments caused some mild side effects like short-term pain after treatment.

However, other trials didn't find clear differences between manual therapy and exercise and other treatments like injections or surgery. Some trials suggested that combining manual therapy or exercise with other treatments might not offer extra benefits.

Overall, the evidence suggests that manual therapy and exercise can help with pain and function, but it's not clear if they're better than other treatments. More research is needed to confirm these findings and to see if different types of manual therapy or exercise work best. Future studies should compare these treatments to realistic placebos and have a strong reason for doing so.

output: This review looked at seven studies, mostly in children, to see if removing their tonsils and adenoids (a procedure called adeno-/tonsillectomy) helps reduce sore throats. In children, those who had the surgery had fewer sore throats overall, especially those who were more sick. They had about 0.6 fewer sore throats in the first year after the surgery compared to those who didn't have the surgery. However, the difference was small, and one sore throat often happened right after the surgery. For adults, the studies were shorter and mixed, so we can't be sure if the surgery helps. More research is needed to know if the surgery is worth doing for sore throats.

output: This review looked at whether giving antibiotics later instead of right away helps with symptoms like fever, pain, and cough in people with certain types of respiratory infections. It included 11 studies with a total of 3555 participants. Most studies were done in doctor's offices or clinics. The studies found that giving antibiotics later didn't seem to make much difference in how sick people felt or how quickly they got better. However, it did help reduce the number of antibiotics given out. Patients who waited for antibiotics to start feeling better were just as satisfied as those who got them right away. The review suggests that waiting to give antibiotics might be a good idea for some people with respiratory infections because it can help stop the spread of bacteria that cause infections, which can lead to less antibiotic resistance. This means fewer people would get sick again from the same bacteria.
